thread.title: Can Tesla, Musk Turn Model 3 Into A Profit Driver?| Investor's Business Daily

author: BRIAN DEAGON
title: Can Tesla, Musk Turn Model 3 Into A Profit Driver?| Investor's Business Daily
text:
While Tesla ( TSLA ) and Chief Executive Elon Musk offered a glowing assessment this past week on Model 3 vehicle production, missing from that report was any word about whether the electric car maker can operate in the black.
X
What made the omission unusual is that Musk has been saying for months that a Tesla profit would be coming by the third or fourth quarter. He said so as recently as Sept. 29, in an email to employees.
"We are very close to achieving profitability and proving the naysayers wrong, but, to be certain, we must execute really well tomorrow (Sunday)," he wrote. "If we go all out tomorrow, we will achieve an epic victory beyond all expectations."
That Sunday he referenced was Sept. 30, the final day of the third quarter. The following Tuesday, Tesla issued its quarterly report on production and deliveries of its all-electric vehicles. Focused mainly on the Model 3, it was a positive report overall.

Please contact customer service CLOSE But there was little indication that Musk will live up to his oft-repeated stand. All the company had to say about a Tesla profit was that "net income and cash flow results will be announced along with the rest of our financial performance when we announce Q3 earnings."
Hitting High End On Model 3 Tesla said it produced 80,142 electric vehicles in the third quarter, 50% more than it built in the second quarter and hitting the high end of estimates. It produced 53,239 Tesla Model 3 cars, coming in at the high end of guidance and almost double the volume of the second quarter.
"With production stabilized, delivery and outbound vehicle logistics were our main challenges during Q3," the announcement said. "We made many improvements to these processes throughout the quarter, and plan to make further improvements in Q4 so that we can scale successfully."
The company is expected to report third-quarter results around the end of this month. Musk has said that a Tesla profit would come on a GAAP basis, referring to the standard generally accepted accounting principles.
Some analysts expect the company to be profitable on a non-GAAP, adjusted earnings basis. But doing so on GAAP basis is a higher mountain to climb.
A Tesla profit has come during only two quarters in its history.
Lack Of Tesla Profit Commentary RBC Capital Markets analyst Joseph Spak says he remains concerned about the company's profitability.
"We still have a difficult time seeing GAAP profitability in the quarter," Spak wrote in a note to clients.
Nomura analyst Romit Shah said Tesla's third-quarter production report exceeded analyst estimates across the board. He added, though, its lack of commentary on profitability was a disappointment.
"We anticipate that the stock could remain rangebound until there is more clarity on Tesla's profitability and cash position," he wrote in his note to clients. Shah maintained a neutral rating on the stock with a price target of 300.
"If Tesla can exhibit profitability and an improved cash position over the next 3-6 months, we believe the stock could move meaningfully higher," Shah wrote.
Reasons For Doubt On Tesla Profit Goal There are reasons to doubt Musk can live up to his assurances that Tesla will be profitable this year.
Model 3 production in the third quarter met goals overall. But the company failed to reach a goal of 5,000 to 6,000 Model 3 cars per week. Musk has said reaching that production level on a consistent basis is important to becoming profitable.
Also clouding the forecast is what Musk has called a "delivery logistics hell" issue. Tesla is having a difficult time getting its cars to customers who want to buy them. The delivery problems could hurt its bottom line. The company can book revenue only when it puts cars into the hands of customers.
Another emerging challenge facing Tesla are the trade disputes between the U.S. and China. These have resulted in Tesla's vehicles being subject to 40% tariffs, up from 25%. It's also well above the 15% levied on most other imported vehicles. Additionally, Tesla vehicles are ineligible for incentives provided to electric vehicle manufacturers that produce vehicles locally in China.
Losing Ground In China With transport costs and tariffs, Tesla now operates at a 55%-60% cost disadvantage compared with cars produced in China. This makes for a challenging competitive environment, given that China is by far the largest market for electric vehicles.
To address this issue, the company is accelerating construction of its China-based factory in Shanghai .
How Tesla plans to implement manufacturing expansion and the capital expenditures that go with it will also play into profitability. Tesla continues to expand its manufacturing plant in Fremont, Calif. It also continues work on expanding its massive battery manufacturing plant in Nevada .
Two new car manufacturing factories are in the planning stages. One will be built at a location not yet revealed in Europe and the other in Shanghai.
Tesla's Debt Load Turning a profit now is critical for Tesla. The company is burning through about $1 billion in cash every three months. At the end of June, it had $2.2 billion in the bank. This amount had dropped to $1.69 billion by Aug. 12 due to a $500 million payment on its revolving credit line
A total of $2.7 billion of Tesla debt is due this year and next, according to Goldman Sachs. Tesla has about $11 billion in total debt. In the company's second-quarter earnings call, Musk said the company would not need to raise additional capital.
"Given the precarious balance sheet, we remain skeptical of that claim," Needham analyst Rajvindra Gill wrote in a note to clients last week.
Musk's profit goal also has been buffeted by a steady string of executive departures over the past 18 months. Last month, Dave Morton resigned as Tesla's chief accounting officer, after one month on the job.
Others who left the company include Doug Field, senior vice president of engineering, who returned to Apple ( AAPL ). Also leaving was Jim Keller, who ran Tesla's Autopilot program.
Increased Competition All of this is happening in the midst of increased competition . A number of large automakers are coming to market with all-electric vehicles, ratcheting up the pressure on Musk and Tesla.
Analysts see performance and pricing matching up well with Tesla's Model S, Model X and Model 3. These automakers hope to challenge Tesla's current dominance in the electric vehicle market for the first time.
The first one to hit the market is the Jaguar I-Pace, a product of Tata Motors ( TTM ), to be followed by the Audi e-tron from Volkswagen ( VWAGY ). Others coming to market are the Mercedes-Benz EQC from Daimler ( DDAIF ), the BMW ( BMWYY ) iX3 and the Porsche Taycan, also from Volkswagen.
Edmunds.com analyst Jeremy Acevedo says Musk has plenty to worry about on that front alone.
"They're compelling vehicles and they certainly could take market share away from Tesla," he said.
